newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds marked down in marginal trade.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds marked down in marginal trade.

text.p: Irish bonds were marked lower in marginal trade on Tuesday as business resumed after the St Patrick's Day holiday, dealers said.
"The market's a bit ropey," one dealer said.

"We were marked down one and a half points in the first hour of trading due to the double knock of EMU delay fears in Europe and the fall in sterling triggered by the announcement of the UK election date."
Dealers said however that there was interest in the market at lower price levels.

By 1600 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 80 pence from Tuesday's close to 100.85 to yield 6.27 percent while the benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 1.78 Irish pounds from Friday's close at 107.05 to yield 6.94 percent.
Dealers said the auction of 150 million Irish pounds of the eight percent bond due 2006 by Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency on Tuesday had gone very well.

"The issue was three times over-subscribed," a dealer said. "We had to cheapen up a good bit - underperforming bunds by about ten basis points at one stage - but it meant the bonds went at better levels for investors."
The fact that the auction had gone well could lead to some bounce on spreads in the short term, dealers said.
Looking ahead it was important that fears over a delay in the timetable for EMU were allayed, dealers said, otherwise the Irish market and other non-core markets would struggle.
The NTMA said on Tuesday that the highest price achieved was 107.05 pounds, to yield 6.95 percent and the lowest accepted price was 106.85 to yield 6.97 percent.
Bidders at the lowest accepted price were allocated 10 percent of the bid at that price, the NTMA said.
The NTMA said 30 million punts of stock was available in a non-competitive auction.
Elsewhere UK gilt futures were steady at lower levels after the UK February PBSR came in at deficit of 3.6 billion pounds sterling against a market expectation of 3.7 billion pounds.
